findings.title: Findings converge on D6's claim pass over HSL901's own diagnostics
findings.why_it_matters: D6 (option C, ratified) adds a pass where pragmas claim HSL901 diagnostics. Both critics, from different angles, found that the ledger describes this pass in one sentence and leaves its mechanics open. It doesn't say how the pass relates to the existing claim engine (`_collect_claims`/`_owns`), which pragma "about that same pragma" means, how pragmas naming HSL901 avoid being reported as unused or overlapping, or where the pass sits relative to the per-file diagnostic budget. Each finding proposes its own local specification. Should the claim pass itself be re-evaluated instead of patched point by point? Open questions a re-evaluation would answer: does the pass need to exist given no known inline use case (D6's own table says "none known here"), does it need to be a separate mechanism or a re-run of the existing one, and are its edge cases worth specifying or better accepted as limitations.
findings.recommended: B: Keep D6's claim pass and address Findings 2 and 3 individually.
findings.chosen: B: Keep D6's claim pass and address Findings 2 and 3 individually.

findings.title: D6's claim mechanism, its scope, and the handling of pragmas naming HSL901 are unspecified
findings.why_it_matters: As written, D6 invites a second resolver beside `_collect_claims`/`_owns` that matches diagnostics to "that same pragma." The diagnostics carry no link to a pragma: `_diagnostic` builds them with `SourceKind.NO_OWNER` and no owner. The existing code also gives a pragma naming HSL901 the wrong result. With HSL901 enabled, `scan_pragmas` accepts the pragma and `_collect_claims` builds a claim whose candidates come from file-rule findings. Those findings never carry HSL901, so the claim is empty and gets `unused suppression for HSL901`. The ledger states the outcome ("never reported unused") but not where the exemption lives. Overlap is also open. If `ignore-file[HSL901]` and a statement `ignore[HSL901]` both claim one HSL901 diagnostic, the overlap is itself an HSL901 "redundant" diagnostic that both of them would claim, so the reporting is circular. The scope of "about itself" is ambiguous too. If diagnostics carry the pragma's statement owner and the existing `_owns` resolves them, then `ignore[HSL901]` on a multi-line statement claims the diagnostics of every pragma on that statement, and `ignore-next[HSL901]` stacked above another `ignore-next[HSL002]` for the same statement claims that pragma's diagnostics. Matching the literal ratified wording instead needs a pragma-identity match that `_owns` doesn't have. Finally, the ledger doesn't say whether suppressed HSL901 diagnostics count toward `suppressed_count`. Today that count only covers candidates (`suppressions.py:123-132`), so the user-facing "N suppressed" number changes if they are counted.
findings.recommended: B: Build HSL901 diagnostics with the pragma's owner (and not `NO_OWNER`), run the existing claim resolution over them once, and reword D6's scope to "a statement pragma listing HSL901 claims the HSL901 diagnostics on pragmas with the same statement owner." Record in D6 that pragmas naming HSL901 never enter unused or overlap reporting (like project-rule pragmas, `suppressions.py:214`), and that suppressed HSL901 diagnostics don't count in `suppressed_count`, since they were never candidates.
findings.chosen: B: Build HSL901 diagnostics with the pragma's owner (and not NO_OWNER), run the existing claim resolution over them once, and reword D6's scope.

findings.title: The D6 claim pass's position relative to the per-file diagnostic budget is unstated
findings.why_it_matters: `apply_suppressions` adds every diagnostic through `add_diagnostic`, which counts against `limit - len(candidates)` and raises `SuppressionBudgetExceeded` once the limit is passed. If HSL901 diagnostics are added as they are generated and only claimed afterwards, a file whose HSL901 diagnostics are all suppressed by `ignore-file[HSL901]` can still trip the budget, producing a `candidate budget` error and a truncated result. The recovery path (`_recover_candidate_budget`) calls the same `apply_suppressions`, so a claim pass that lives inside that function covers both paths.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a file with more than ~10,000 suppression diagnostics can report a candidate-budget error even when `ignore-file[HSL901]` suppresses them.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation

findings.title: D4's "deleting the flagged pragmas is safe" invariant depends on `_owns`'s window shape and is unrecorded
findings.why_it_matters: D4-B (report all but one overlapping pragma, the broader scope surviving and then the earlier one) is safe only because the claim sets nest. `ignore-file` claims every candidate of its rule. `ignore-next` claims its statement's candidates plus the `NO_OWNER` window, so it contains any trailing `ignore` on the same statement. An earlier `ignore-next`'s window contains a later one's, and pragmas with the same target have identical sets. So the survivor's set always contains every flagged pragma's set, and deleting the flagged pragmas changes nothing that is suppressed. That invariant is the whole justification for D4-B, and it lives in `_owns`, which has already grown a special case (the `NO_OWNER` window). If `_owns` widens later, D4's promise breaks silently.
findings.chosen: In D4, add one sentence recording the invariant: the survivor's claim set contains every flagged pragma's set, because claim sets nest (file ⊇ statement; an `ignore-next` ⊇ a trailing `ignore` on its statement; an earlier `ignore-next` window ⊇ a later one's). Add a build item: a test over overlap fixtures asserting the suppressed-candidate set is identical before and after removing every pragma HSL901 flags as redundant.

findings.title: D4 leaves the all-unused overlap and multi-ID pragmas undefined
findings.why_it_matters: Today a pragma in a conflict gets the conflict message instead of "unused" (`if index in conflicts ... elif not claim.candidates`). D4 doesn't say what happens in two cases. First, two overlapping pragmas that both have no candidates, for example two `ignore-file[HSL002]` in a file with no HSL002 findings: they overlap by target even with nothing to suppress. Is the survivor also reported unused? If it isn't, cleanup takes two runs. Second, a multi-ID pragma where only one ID overlaps: the diagnostic sits on the whole comment, so D4's "delete the pragma it points at" is wrong for `ignore[HSL002, HSL003]`, where the user should remove the ID, not the pragma. The obvious implementation (a redundant claim reports only `redundant`, any other claim reports `unused` when its candidates are empty) already gives both reports in one run.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: D4 leaves the all-unused overlap and multi-ID wording to the build.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation

findings.title: D5-A as worded can't be built as a plain field move, and it weakens `ProjectRule`'s required `languages`
findings.why_it_matters: `Rule`'s only defaulted field is `base_match` (`kw_only=True`). `FileRule` and `ProjectRule` follow it with the non-default fields `detect` and `run`. A defaulted `languages` on the base, empty so HSL900's row stays as written, must be keyword-only or the dataclass fails with "non-default argument follows default argument." Once it is keyword-only and defaulted, `ProjectRule.languages` stops being required. A project-rule row that omits it compiles, gets an empty set, is dropped from every file by `applicable_rules`, and is left out of `discovered_languages`, so the rule never runs and nothing says why. The current required field prevents exactly that. The base's empty default also contradicts `FileRule`'s Python default. D5's cost line ("a field move that touches each rule kind") understates this.
findings.recommended: A: Make `languages` a required, keyword-only field on `Rule`. HSL900's row states `languages=frozenset()`, the file-rule helpers supply Python, and the project-rule helpers pass it by keyword. Update D5's cost line to say this.
findings.chosen: A: Make languages a required, keyword-only field on Rule.

findings.title: HSL901 never reports stale or redundant project-rule pragmas
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: other users reading "stale suppression" docs; the maintainer knows spec 010 D9. Project-rule pragmas stay exempt from unused and overlap reporting, so even with `extend-select = ["HSL901"]`, a stale `ignore[HSL104]` is never found, and `ignore-file[HSL104]` plus `ignore[HSL104]` is never reported as redundant. The disabled-rule diagnostic does apply to project rules, which makes the asymmetry easier to notice. A rule named for stale suppressions might suggest otherwise.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: HSL901 doesn't report stale or redundant project-rule pragmas (spec 010 D9), as `docs/suppressions.md` already says.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation
